sentences.text: Conservation is expensive, and with limited money and effort, societies must constantly decide which species are worth the cost of saving.
One proposed rule would draw the line by cause, saving species only when human activity is to blame for their decline and letting so-called natural extinctions run their course.
Although the policy carries a certain moral logic, I believe its consequences would be harmful, because the value of saving a species rarely depends on what caused its decline.

sections.role: Body — The cause is rarely separable

sentences.text: First, implementing the policy would force conservationists into nearly impossible judgments about cause.
In a world reshaped by human agriculture, climate change, and travel, almost no extinction is purely natural, and disentangling human from non-human causes is often impossible.
Officials would waste scarce time and money litigating blame instead of protecting habitats, and many species would vanish while the argument dragged on.
Did the fish die because of the new dam, the warming river, or a parasite that has always lurked in these waters, and who could honestly say?
A policy that hinges on an unanswerable question is a recipe for paralysis.
More importantly, the consequences of losing a species do not change according to why it is disappearing.
A bee that vanishes through some natural shift still leaves crops unpollinated, and a predator lost to disease still allows its prey to multiply and unbalance the ecosystem.
Nature is a web of dependencies, and removing a strand weakens the whole regardless of cause, so a policy indifferent to natural extinctions would let real and avoidable damage unfold.
To stand by and watch, merely because the first domino fell without our help, is to mistake passivity for innocence.
The loss of a single keystone species can cascade through an entire landscape, toppling others that quietly depended on it.
If the practical harm is the same, the reason to act is the same.
The strongest case for the policy is moral: that humans bear special responsibility for the harm they cause and none for nature's own workings.
There is something to this, and where humans have driven a species toward extinction, the duty to act is especially clear and urgent.
But responsibility for causing harm is a reason to do more, not a license to do nothing whenever we happen to be blameless.
If we have the power to prevent a catastrophe and decline merely because we did not start it, the resulting loss is one we have allowed all the same.
A lifeguard does not refuse to save a drowning swimmer simply because he was not the one who pushed the man into the sea.
Our obligation flows from our ability to help, not only from our guilt in causing harm.
In conclusion, restricting conservation to human-caused extinctions would do real damage for the sake of a tidy principle.
The cause of a species' decline may help set priorities, but it should not be the gatekeeper that decides whether we act at all.
What we can save, and what it is worth, should weigh far more heavily than the question of original blame.
Faced with a preventable loss, the wiser policy asks not whose fault it is, but whether saving the species is worth the cost and within our power.
